task_brief: This is day 6 of "Typing and Getting Organized". That is unit 3 in grade 3. Today is a correction and reflection about basic word processing. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Create and save one clearly named, organized digital or paper folder of practice work. Today helps by working on basic word processing. Your unit also covers home row typing basics, saving a file, naming files clearly, and finding a saved file. Today adds real evidence toward your unit project.
primary_task: Look back at your earlier work on basic word processing and fix it. Make a fix-it list. For each mistake write four things: what went wrong, why it went wrong, what you changed, and how you know it works now. Include one thing that failed before and works now. Then look at all your mistakes together. What do they have in common? Name one habit that would catch it sooner. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about basic word processing. It is part of "Typing and Getting Organized". Later days in this unit cover other things, like home row typing basics. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about basic word processing; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

concept_teaching.title: Follow evidence across a system boundary: basic word processing
concept_teaching.entry_check: Before reading, write one prediction about basic word processing and one observation that could show the prediction is wrong. This readiness record is no-penalty evidence.
explanation: basic word processing is about making a clear choice and showing why it works. First name what the result should do. Then point to the step, label, or fact that supports your choice.
A check is different from a guess. Write what you expect before you try it. Compare what happened with what you expected. If they differ, circle the first place they stop matching.
A fix needs a reason. Change one thing that your evidence supports, try the same checks again, and keep the old and new work. That record shows your thinking even when the first try was wrong.

Trace input, processing, storage, and output in order. Locate the first boundary whose observed state differs from its specified state before proposing a repair. You may use paper, objects, labelled drawings, or precise steps when a computer is not the best tool.

key_terms.definition: A named part with a defined responsibility.
The information a component holds at a particular moment.

worked_example.title: Worked analogue: count ready cards without skipping evidence
worked_example.goal: Return the number of fictional cards whose ready field is true.
worked_example.public_observation: For [{ready: true}, {ready: false}, {ready: true}], expected is 2 but actual is 4. For [], expected and actual are both 0.

annotations.reasoning: Each ready card contributes exactly one to the count; a non-ready card contributes zero.
After the first ready card, total should be 1. Write that state before tracing.
The first iteration changes total from 0 to 2, so the first divergence is the state update, not the loop boundary or return.
Change the ready-card update so it adds one. This predicts totals 1, 1, and 2 across the three iterations.
The mixed case returns 2, [] returns 0, and three ready cards return 3. All expected and actual results match.

worked_example.correctness_and_efficiency: After each iteration, total equals the number of ready cards in the prefix already examined. The invariant begins true for the empty prefix, one iteration maintains it, and termination covers the whole list. Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
worked_example.transfer_prompt: On the protected task, identify its own first divergent state. Do not copy this update: the protected fixture uses a different data shape and defect.
worked_example.difference_from_protected_task: This model counts object flags and repairs an over-large accumulator update. The protected task uses different inputs, behavior, identifiers, and a separately withheld resolution.

guided_task.support_fade: Prompts identify the state and evidence order here. The protected independent task supplies only its specification, public checks, and a location/evidence cue; the fresh check permits term or instruction clarification only.

debugging_reasoning.title: Use the six-move evidence cycle
required_moves: Symptom: record expected versus actual without explaining it away.
Hypothesis: state one falsifiable cause about the program state before revising.
Inspection: identify the first trace row or printed detail that bears on the hypothesis.
Predicted effect: state what one controlled change should alter and what it should leave unchanged.
Test and interpretation: compare actual with the prediction and mark the hypothesis supported, rejected, or not fully tested.
Verification: rerun all relevant checks and record any new limitation or next hypothesis.
debugging_reasoning.anti_guessing_rule: A working final artifact without a pre-change hypothesis and inspectable evidence is incomplete debugging/revision evidence.

remediation_routes.learner_signal: My explanation repeats the final goal but does not describe what is true partway through execution.
remediation_routes.title: Different representation: token-and-box state walk
remediation_routes.alternate_teaching: Represent each variable or collection with a labelled box and move one token per executed step. After every move, write one sentence that must still be true. This makes partial state visible without showing the protected repair.
remediation_routes.analogue_task: Walk through a three-step fictional counter with tokens and state what is true after steps one and two; do not use the protected identifiers or inputs.
remediation_routes.return_check: Complete the fresh mastery check with teaching materials closed. The original protected solution remains withheld.

remediation_routes.learner_signal: I changed or chose something before recording the mismatch and a testable reason.
remediation_routes.title: Different routine: the six-box evidence ladder
remediation_routes.alternate_teaching: Use six boxes in order: expected/actual, first divergence or decisive detail, hypothesis, predicted effect, one revision, rerun interpretation. Do not enter the revision box until the first four constrain what the change is meant to test.
remediation_routes.analogue_task: Apply the six boxes to a separate fictional clock-card mismatch related to basic word processing. Stop after the prediction, explain what result would reject the hypothesis, then finish the check.
remediation_routes.return_check: Complete the fresh mastery check independently. A correct but low-confidence response receives confirmation tied to evidence, not automatic reteaching.

fresh_mastery_check.evidence_requirements: Submit a new six-move log, corrected code or precise pseudocode, every public rerun, a prefix-state invariant, and time/extra-space reasoning.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

remediation: Reteaching for basic word processing follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for basic word processing, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for basic word processing works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of basic word processing, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking basic word processing mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply basic word processing under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on basic word processing rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
